summary: Provides for associating tags with YANG modules to classify and organize them. It gives a method to define, read and write tags, which may be registered, assigned by implementations or set by users, and offers guidance to model writers.

eli5.summary: Stickers on books so you can find them by topic. This does it for network model files.

how do i remove a tag from a yang module
what is a masked-tag in yang
subtitle: A simple tagging scheme for classifying YANG modules, with registered, vendor and user-defined tags.

tldr.problem: Devices and repositories hold many YANG modules, and there is no flexible way to classify or filter them by topic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8819 defines a YANG module that attaches string tags to module names, a module-tag extension for design-time tags, and IANA registries for tag prefixes and IETF tags.
tldr.outcome: Users, vendors and the IETF can all label modules, and users can mask any tag they do not want. The RFC itself defines no actions based on tags.

today: RFC 8819 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It updates RFC 8407, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Tag YANG Modules
sections.content:
Tags are a flexible way to organize things, and the RFC compares them to internet hashtags. Unlike a rigid structure, tags adapt more easily as technologies change. RFC 8819 defines a YANG module that holds a list of module entries, so tags can be added, removed and viewed for each module. It follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342.

The RFC lists some possible uses. A device could list all vendor modules with an XPath query. Several management clients could coordinate, for example by marking modules that have not been verified. A repository search for the ietf:routing tag could return only IETF routing modules. Future protocol extensions could filter queries by tag.

The document also updates RFC 8407, the guidelines for authors of YANG data models.
sections.eli5: Tags are like hashtags. They let you find the files you care about without memorising every file name.

sections.title: Tag Values and Prefixes
sections.content:
All tags SHOULD begin with a prefix that says who owns their definition. Apart from that prefix, the RFC deliberately puts no structure on the value. A tag can contain any YANG string characters except carriage returns, newlines and tabs.

  • ietf: tags are all registered with IANA.
  • vendor: tags are defined by the vendor that implements the module and are not registered. Vendors are RECOMMENDED to add extra identification, such as an organization name, to avoid collisions (for example vendor:example.com:vendor-defined-classifier).
  • user: tags are defined by the user or administrator and are not meant to be registered. Using the prefix is RECOMMENDED but not required.

Any tag that starts with none of these prefixes is reserved for future use. Such tags are not invalid, only reserved in the context of specifications such as RFCs.
sections.eli5: Each sticker starts with a short word that says who made it: the standards group, the company, or you. That way two people do not accidentally use the same sticker for different things.

sections.title: How Tags Get Attached
sections.content:
A tag can become associated with a module at design time, at implementation time, or through user control. Because users are the main consumers of tags, a user may remove any tag, however it got there.

Module definition tagging: a module author MAY list tags with the module-tag extension statement. If the module is defined in an IETF Standards Track document, those tags MUST be IETF tags. The IANA registry then acts as a check against duplicates.

Implementation tagging: an implementation MAY add more tags, which SHOULD be IETF tags or vendor tags.

User tagging: users can assign and remove tags of any kind through normal configuration. To remove a tag from the operational datastore, the user adds a matching masked-tag entry for the module.
sections.eli5: The book's author can put a sticker on, the shop can add more, and you can add your own. If you do not like a sticker, you can mark it as hidden for you.

sections.title: The ietf-module-tags Module
sections.content:
The module ietf-module-tags has a module-tags container with a list named module, keyed by name (a YANG identifier). Each entry has a leaf-list of tag values and a leaf-list of masked-tag values. A tag is a string of at least one character with no carriage return, newline or tab.

The operational view of an entry's tags is built in three steps: add system tags (those from the module-tag extension or the implementation), add user-configured tags, then remove any tag equal to a masked tag. It is not an error to mask a tag the module does not have, but it has no effect.

The module-tag extension takes one argument, a tag, and marks tags that SHOULD be added automatically by the system, with origin system.

Appendix B adds a temporary non-NMDA module, ietf-module-tags-state, whose containers are marked deprecated, for implementations that do not yet support NMDA.
sections.eli5: The model is a list of files, each with a pile of stickers and a pile of hidden stickers. What you finally see is the stickers minus the hidden ones.

sections.title: The IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created a YANG Module Tag Prefixes registry. Its allocation policy is Specification Required (RFC 8126). Prefixes are short strings of lowercase ASCII alphanumerics ending in a colon. The initial entries are ietf:, vendor: and user:. Other standards bodies that want their own tags should allocate a prefix.

The IETF YANG Module Tags registry allocates tags with the ietf: prefix under IETF Review. New values should be well considered and not achievable by combining existing tags, and they must conform to Net-Unicode (RFC 5198).

The initial tags include five that mirror the classification of RFC 8199 (such as ietf:network-element-class and ietf:sdo-defined-class) and topic tags such as ietf:routing, ietf:security, ietf:qos, ietf:oam and ietf:system-management. IANA also registered the XML namespaces and the two module names.

For IETF-standardized modules, new tags MUST be assigned in this registry.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of approved sticker words and a list of approved starting words. Anyone writing a new standard sticker has to add it to the official list first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF, whose lowest layer is a secure transport, with Secure Shell (SSH) mandatory to implement.

The RFC adds only metadata and defines no action based on it, so it says it does not by itself introduce new security considerations. People who define actions on top of tags need to weigh the security implications of their actions, including the chance that one user masks a tag another relies on.
sections.eli5: Stickers are only labels, so they are not dangerous alone. But if a machine does something because of a sticker, someone hiding that sticker could change what happens.

items.label: IETF tags
items.desc: Registered with IANA in the IETF YANG Module Tags registry.

items.label: Vendor tags
items.desc: Defined by the module implementer; not registered.

items.label: User tags
items.desc: Defined by and for the user; not meant to be registered.
